title: Interview with Simon Davidmann, AI + EDA Researcher and Former CEO of Imperas - Semiwiki
gist: Simon Davidmann, whose five EDA ventures were all absorbed by Cadence, Viewlogic or Synopsys (Imperas in 2023), argues the chip design ecosystem is 'blinded by the LLMs headlights' — using AI to run legacy flows faster rather than changing what can be designed and verified. He offers a Dilemma/Test framework, cites ML verification results spanning 85% less RTL simulation to 10% better coverage, and calls today's agentic EDA tools a band-aid ahead of a full design/verification/implementation architectural reset.

insights.claim: Every company Simon Davidmann founded or helped build since the early 1980s was acquired by a larger EDA tools firm: Gateway Design Automation by Cadence in 1991, Chronologic Simulation (developer of VCS) by Viewlogic in 1995 and then Synopsys, Ambit Design Systems by Cadence in 1998 for $280 million, Co-Design by Synopsys in 2002, and Imperas by Synopsys in 2023.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The structural exit path in EDA is acquisition by the Big Three, not independent scaling — price new EDA/verification startups as M&A optionality for Synopsys and Cadence rather than standalone compounders.
insights.quote: Each of the companies Davidmann founded or was a key staff member of since the early 1980s has been acquired by a larger EDA tools firms
insights.locator: Davidmann has an illustrious track record

insights.claim: The Superlog language co-architected at Co-Design was a superset of Verilog that became the IEEE standard SystemVerilog, showing that de facto EDA language standards have historically originated in small startups and were then bought by incumbents.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Standards capture, not tool features, is where durable EDA franchise value is created — watch which startup formats/languages are being pulled into standards bodies today.
insights.locator: he founded Co-Design and co-architected the Superlog language

insights.claim: Davidmann left Synopsys in 2025 after serving as Vice President responsible for Processor Modeling and Simulation and is now an AI + EDA researcher at Southampton University in the UK.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A senior Synopsys processor-modeling leader moving to academia to rethink verification is an early tell that the next architecture shift is being incubated outside incumbent roadmaps.

themes.theme: RISC-V custom silicon pulling verification demand

insights.claim: Imperas built reference models of Arm and RISC-V processors for virtual platforms including Open Virtual Platforms and Synopsys Virtualizer, and its ImperasDV pioneered asynchronous lock-step oracle verification to catch the most complex processor bugs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Reference-model plus lock-step oracle is the incumbent methodology any RISC-V verification challenger must beat; it is now inside Synopsys.
insights.locator: For the past many years, I was CEO of Imperas

insights.claim: From 2016 onward an increasing share of RISC-V verification users were building custom silicon for custom workloads, with Nvidia and Denso cited as examples of firms building what would now be called AI accelerators.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Custom-accelerator proliferation, not merchant CPU volume, is the demand driver for processor verification IP — a tailwind for tools priced per design program rather than per wafer.
insights.locator: When we started working with RISC-V back in 2016

insights.claim: AI hardware requires simulation volumes large enough that handling them was itself a research problem, meaning accelerator design consumes compute capacity in verification before any chip ships.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Compute demand from pre-silicon verification of AI chips is a second-order buyer of servers and emulation hardware, separate from training and inference demand.
insights.quote: Part of this interest was simply learning how we could handle such large amounts of simulation needed by this AI hardware.
insights.locator: Part of this interest was simply learning

themes.theme: Measured ML gains in verification today

insights.claim: A review of ML-in-verification products and academic adopters presented at a DVClub event showed results ranging from 85% less RTL simulation required to 10% better coverage achieved.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Concrete efficiency benchmarks to hold EDA vendors' AI claims against; an 85% simulation reduction also implies deflation risk for compute-metered verification revenue.
insights.quote: results ranged from 85% less RTL simulation required, to 10% better coverage achieved
insights.locator: I recently presented at a DVClub event

insights.claim: EDA tools have been absorbing advanced optimization mathematics and machine learning for roughly the last ten years, so current AI adoption in verification is an incremental continuation rather than a step change.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Discount vendor narratives that frame 2026 AI features as novel; the differentiated claim would be architectural change, not more ML inside existing engines.
insights.locator: For years, EDA has done a great job in optimizing design

themes.theme: The LLM blind spot: Dilemma and Test

insights.claim: The chip design ecosystem is 'blinded by the LLMs headlights,' fixating on large language models at the expense of other AI approaches to design and verification.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Contrarian screen for EDA investments: favour teams whose AI thesis is not an LLM wrapper on existing flows.
insights.quote: I think the chip design ecosystem is just “Blinded by the LLMs headlights.”

insights.claim: Davidmann's stated Dilemma is that the chip design ecosystem uses AI to accelerate what it already knows how to do, while the real opportunity is to transform what and how it is possible to design and verify — a systemic tension in which every individual player acting rationally guarantees a collectively wrong outcome.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A coordination-failure framing predicts incumbents will underinvest in the disruptive path, leaving the transformation to startups or academia — where the asymmetric returns sit.
insights.quote: It is a systemic tension where every individual player acting rationally guarantees a collectively wrong outcome.
insights.locator: I see there is a Dilemma

insights.claim: Davidmann's Test for any AI-in-EDA offering is whether it fundamentally changes what you can design and verify rather than only accelerating how fast you run existing flows; tools that only do the latter fail the Test.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A one-line due-diligence filter for AI-EDA pitches and for judging Synopsys/Cadence AI product announcements.
insights.quote: Does AI fundamentally change what you can design and verify, or does it just accelerate how fast you run what you already do? If it only does the latter, it fails the Test.
insights.locator: Along with my Dilemma, I have a related Test

insights.claim: Injecting AI into legacy chip design processes amounts to 'shovelling faster, not changing the shape of the mountain,' implying productivity gains will saturate without a process redesign.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Expect diminishing returns on AI-assisted incremental EDA features, capping the pricing power vendors can extract from them.
insights.quote: they are just shovelling faster, not changing the shape of the mountain
insights.locator: By simply injecting AI into legacy processes

themes.theme: Where the next EDA architecture wins

insights.claim: Traditional verification approaches are unlikely to cope with the complexity of the hardware architectures now being envisaged, which is why Davidmann shifted to researching ML/AI-based alternatives to verification.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Verification is the emerging bottleneck on advanced chip programs; capacity and methodology constraints there gate time-to-market for accelerator startups.
insights.locator: I thought traditional approaches to verification were not likely to cope

insights.claim: The breakthrough EDA opportunity is a holistic toolchain that unifies design, verification and implementation so AI can reason across the entire stack instead of shuttling between fragmented silos built for humans over the last four decades.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Points capital toward full-stack EDA rebuilds rather than point tools; also flags integration as the incumbents' structural weakness given decades of siloed products.
insights.quote: Unifying design, verification, and implementation allows AI to reason across the entire stack, rather than just shuttling between the fragmented silos built for humans over the last four decades.
insights.locator: Are there opportunities for EDA startups

insights.claim: Today's agentic AI in EDA is a band-aid on the way to a genuine design/verification/implementation architectural reset, so there is room for EDA startups that are not agentic AI tools.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Bearish on the current wave of agentic-EDA startups as durable franchises; the reset, not the agents, is where the value accrues.
insights.quote: Today’s agentic AI is simply a band-aid on the way to a genuine design/verification/implementation architectural reset.
insights.locator: Real breakthrough will come from a holistic approach
